h1: CIWA (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol) Calculator
summary: The CIWA (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol) calculator is a free, no-sign-up health tool. Fill in the 10 fields it asks for and it works out cIWA-Ar score straight away, with the formula shown underneath. Think of it as a shortcut for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the CIWA (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol) calculator work?
sections.html:
The CIWA (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol) calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports cIWA-Ar score in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the nausea or vomiting, the tremor and the paroxysmal sweats).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 8 options, such as no (0p), mild nausea, no vomiting (1p) and symptoms more severe (2p). The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 8 options, such as no tremor (0p), not visible, but can be felt fingertip to fingertip (1p) and symptoms more severe (2p). The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 8 options, such as no sweat visible (0p), barely perceptible sweating, palms moist (1p) and symptoms more severe (2pt). The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 8 options, such as no anxiety, at ease (0p), mildly anxious (1p) and symptoms more severe (2p). The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 8 options, such as normal activity (0p), somewhat more than normal activity (1p) and symptoms more severe (2p). The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 8 options, such as none (0p), very mild itching, pins and needles, burning or numbness (1p) and mild itching, pins and needles, burning or numbness (2p). The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 8 options, such as not present (0p), very mild harshness or ability to frighten (1p) and mild harshness or ability to frighten (2p). The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 8 options, such as not present (0p), very mild sensitivity (1p) and mild sensitivity (2p). The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 8 options, such as not present (0p), very mild (1p) and mild (2p). The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 5 options, such as oriented (0p), cannot do serial additions or is uncertain about date (1p) and disoriented for date by no more than 2 calendar days (2p). The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.

10 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the CIWA (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol) calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

CIWA-Ar score=(agitation + anxiety + auditory disturbances + headache + nausea or vomiting + orientation + paroxysmal sweats + tactile disturbances + tremor + visual disturbances)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The CIWA (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol) calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the CIWA (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol) calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns cIWA-Ar score. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the CIWA (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol) calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for a few values, which is 10 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (10 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports CIWA-Ar score = 0. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the CIWA (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol) calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
